items.title: Will mortgage rates nearing 8% force lenders to make cuts or close their doors?
items.description: Mortgage rates are closer to 8% today than 7% — a surprising development for housing professionals considering the optimism for sub-6% rates held by many at the start of 2026. And the dark clouds forming over the market may result in additional negative consequences beyond fewer home sales and closed loans. HousingWire ‘s Mortgage Rates Center showed that 30-year conforming loan rates averaged 7.63% on Tuesday, up 31 basis points in the past two weeks. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) averaged 7.59% — a startling two-week jump of 59 bps — while rates for 30-year jumbo loans rose 45 bps to average 7.85%. “Mortgage rates increased for the sixth straight week, reaching a nearly three-year high. Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance,” Bob Broeksmit , president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), said in a statement last week. While rising rates have been a hindrance to prospective homebuyers for a while, industry experts indicate that the sharp increase in the past few weeks has also taken a financial toll on lenders — many of which are cutting origination forecasts or considering layoffs . “Bond yields are at the highest level they’ve been in a couple of decades. Mortgage rates are at the highest level they’ve been in several years,” said Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage . “ Banks seem to be panicking about the direction of mortgage rates and prophylactically raising rates, even if they don’t have to, just to get out of the fray. We’re going back to a period like in 2022, when rates went up precipitously, and we saw some lenders going out of the market.” Cohn believes that some lenders may be fighting for survival today — and she pointed to the previous rising-rate environment of a few years ago as an indication of what could happen next . “I think that’s the 800-pound gorilla,” Cohn said. “What damage is there going to be to the lending industry?” Among the recent cuts and closures by lenders, Benchmark Mortgage shut down its wholesale and correspondent division to focus on retail lending; New American Funding shed 160 jobs in its consumer-direct channel; and Pennymac cut some lending and fulfillment roles while closing an office in Tennessee . Hector Amendola, president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG , has been through multiple rising-rate cycles. While consumers are being impacted now by reduced affordability, his advice is that a wait-and-see strategy is unlikely to produce better results. “Two years ago, the conversation was, ‘When do we get back to 5%?’ Now people are asking me about 8%, and this week, I’ve heard 9% floated . Fair enough, the number keeps moving, but the advice doesn’t,” Amendola said in a statement. “Nobody knows where rates are headed going into next year, and anyone who tells you they do is selling something. “What I can tell you is that every month somebody spends waiting for a dramatically low rate is another month spent paying your landlord’s mortgage instead of your own.” Combating affordability hurdles In his monthly “3 Points” video, Mat Ishbia, president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), discussed some potential ways to qualify more borrowers and lower the affordability bar. Ishbia lauded the Federal Housing Finance Agency for rolling out VantageScore 4.0 for all loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . He believes that additional credit-scoring models to compete against Classic FICO will help borrowers secure lower loan-level price adjustments ( LLPAs ) and less expensive mortgage insurance. items.title: Fed's Bowman unveils major overhaul of its bank supervision
items.description: Federal Reserve Fed's Bowman unveils major overhaul of its bank supervision By Kate Berry CloseText About Kate twitter kateberry1 mailto kate.berry@arizent.com linkedin kate-berry-aa69353 Published October 06, 2026, 2:57 p.m. EDT | Updated October 06, 2026, 8:29 p.m. EDT 5 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Bloomberg News Key insight: Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said that abandoning Federal Reserve districts in favor of five regional hubs will streamline joint oversight with state regulators. Supporting data: For decades, the Fed relied on complex internal committees, resulting in delayed enforcement and a lack of accountability, according to Bowman. Expert quote: " In practice, these committees became a source for plausible deniability and a disincentive for examiners to take prompt and decisive action to address identified risks." — Michelle Bowman, Fed vice chair for supervision Processing Content Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman laid out a sweeping overhaul of the central bank's supervisory role that involves dismantling a web of internal committees, realigning oversight into five regions and revising the definition of a community bank. In a speech Tuesday morning at the St. Louis Fed's annual community banking research conference, Bowman announced an aggressive revamp, including a reorganization of bank supervision into five regional divisions that follow state lines rather than Federal Reserve Bank district boundaries. The goal is to coordinate directly with state bank supervisors so that each region has a single leader directly responsible for all supervisory activity in that territory, she said. The new model is designed to empower examiners to issue early supervisory findings without getting bogged down by delays, Bowman said. "The Federal Reserve's supervisory approach should not be a mystery," Bowman said in prepared remarks. "Supervisory expectations should be transparent, clear and consistent. A bank should not learn about and then be held accountable for changed expectations during an examination." In addition, the Fed is expanding the definition of a community bank to include certain firms with traditional, non-complex business models, so they are no longer pushed into higher supervisory tiers built for more complex firms. Bowman, a former Kansas state bank commissioner, did not provide details about how the definition of a community bank will change. For the past 15 years, community banks have been defined as those with assets of less than $10 billion. "By expanding the range of institutions treated as community banks that operate using a traditional community bank business model … we will preserve safety and soundness while effectively applying appropriately tailored and risk-calibrated supervision and regulation," Bowman said. Bowman also said the Fed plans to make significant changes to certain regulatory thresholds that it says are outdated. The Fed will consider updates to fixed-dollar asset thresholds in regulations to account for inflation and economic growth, she said. The proposal will increase static thresholds, with a mechanism to update them every five years. Jaret Seiberg, an analyst at TD Cowen, said Tuesday that he believes the Fed has the leeway to make the changes to thresholds that Bowman discussed. He argued that the new regulatory thresholds could be 50% higher than the current ones, which would benefit banks of various sizes. "That means the $100 billion threshold would be $150 billion, the $250 billion would be $375 billion, and the $700 billion would be more than $1 billion," Seiberg wrote in a note to clients. Bowman's critique of the Fed's past supervision has been informed by an external review of the 2023 regional banking crisis that led to the sudden collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, Signature Bank and First Republic Bank. items.title: ARM reset wave set to crest in 2027, hit pockets of borrowers
items.description: A new wave of adjustable-rate mortgage ( ARM ) resets will arrive in 2027, lifting payments for select borrowers but not creating a systemic threat to the mortgage market or the broader U.S. economy, according to newly released data from Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and Optimal Blue . There are now 3.1 million active first-lien ARMs, the highest level in 5 1/2 years, but they account for only 5.6% of all active mortgages , according to Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE. “Because most newer ARMs are still in their introductory periods, only about a third of active ARMs have begun adjusting,” Walden said in a statement. ICE data shows that 84,000 ARMs had reset through July 2026, with another 64,000 scheduled to reset by the end of the year, bringing the 2026 total to 148,000. Resets are projected to rise to 186,020 in 2027 before easing to 154,710 in 2028. These counts will shift as new ARMs are originated and as borrowers refinance, sell or otherwise exit before their first reset. Why 2027 is a focal year ARM usage plunged to about 1% of rate lock volume in December 2020, when fixed mortgage rates hovered near historic lows, according to Optimal Blue lock data, which covers roughly 40% of the market across about 900 lenders. As mortgage rates began climbing in 2022, ARM volume rebounded, led by 5/1 and 7/1 products. ARMs reached 12.6% of total lock volume in October 2022. “We’re probably still six months away from that first batch of ARM borrowers resetting, once the Federal Reserve started raising rates in spring of 2022,” said Brennan O’Connell , director of data solutions at Optimal Blue. During that early 2022 window, ARM borrowers locked in rates well below today’s levels. Optimal Blue data shows average ARM rates of 3.84% at the end of March 2022 and 4.28% at the end of April 2022. “There’s a story throughout 2027 where there will be a fair number of 5/1 ARMs resetting, that could easily be 200 basis points higher than what they’re currently paying,” O’Connell said. More than 90% of ARMs originated since 2022 remain in their introductory fixed periods, ICE data shows. While overall reset counts in 2027 are expected to remain limited in the context of the broader market, individual borrowers could see meaningful payment changes. Among the more exposed groups are roughly 74,000 seven-year ARMs originated in 2020. These loans are expected to experience the largest median payment increase, at about $1,066 per month, or 36%, reflecting their lower initial rates, larger balances and higher periodic rate caps. Another 65,000 borrowers with five-year ARMs originated in 2022 will experience a change of $430 (+22%). Post-crisis safeguards ARM popularity tends to increase alongside mortgage rates because the products typically offer lower initial payments than fixed-rate loans. The upfront relief, however, can come with exposure to higher payments when the introductory period ends. With the Fed beginning to raise rates , ICE data shows ARMs recently accounted for more than 11% of mortgage rate locks, their largest share in nearly four years. ICE’s conforming 30-year fixed rate index reached 7.2% on Sept. 24. But today’s ARM borrowers are generally better positioned than those who took out similar loans before the 2008 financial crisis. Post-crisis underwriting standards typically require borrowers to qualify at the fully indexed rate rather than just the initial teaser rate, reducing the likelihood of severe payment shock and default when rates adjust. ICE expects the Fed’s most recent rate hike to have only a modest and gradual impact on most existing ARM borrowers. Assuming a full 25-basis-point pass-through to underlying ARM indexes, the median affected borrower would see their monthly payment rise by about $14, according to ICE. More recently originated ARMs, which tend to have higher loan balances, could see a median increase of roughly $53 per month. Related More: Adjustable-Rate Mortga

items.title: Bipartisan group wants ‘more pro-housing legislation’: Rep. Harder
items.description: An article from Bipartisan group wants ‘more pro-housing legislation’: Rep. Harder California Rep. Josh Harder told Multifamily Dive that the Build America Caucus’ policy package aims to “kickstart the conversation of what comes next after ROAD [to Housing].” Published Oct. 6, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Listen to the article 5 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . The bipartisan Build America Caucus, which helped spearhead passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing law, on Monday released the Build More Agenda , a package of more than 60 policy proposals addressing housing and other topics, according to an Oct. 5 press release. Reps. Josh Harder (D-Calif.) and Celeste Maloy (R-Utah) are leading the effort in response “to the dysfunction that has kept us from building the things that are integral to American life,” per the release. Founded in 2025, the Build America Caucus aims to “advance federal pro-growth policies and make it easier to build,” according to its website. The goal of these new proposals is to "kickstart the conversation of what comes next after ROAD,” Harder told Multifamily Dive. “We don't want to rest on our laurels, and we've proven that there's a bipartisan coalition of folks that want to do more pro-housing legislation,” Harder said. “This is a set of ideas that get people excited and thinking about what can come next, and our hope is to flesh it out over the next couple of months and work on it next Congress.” Besides pushing for implementation of ROAD, the caucus is focused on measures that the law didn’t comprehensively address, such as development financing, restrictive zoning, building codes and streamlining federal housing systems, according to Harder. Financing is a focus “because there wasn't a whole lot of that in the bill,” he said. “We know that as interest rates have continued to go up, that projects can’t move forward without reliable and affordable financing,” Harder said. “It’s very clear that high [interest] rates are hurting housing starts…. and I think we have a real opportunity to fix that.” To that end, the group wants to establish a federal revolving loan fund for housing, which Harder thinks can be done at “basically no cost to the federal government.” “By putting in some initial dollars, doing loans to housing projects at below-market-rate interest, and then making sure that those loans are repaid and creating that revolving fund, I think that's going to be a really important vehicle towards filling some of the financing gaps for the construction of more housing,” Harder said. The group also wants to speed up multifamily lending by modernizing HUD systems and underwriting processes. Specifically, it wants to streamline the Federal Housing Agency’s financing process for infill housing. “Those FHA loans can take a year to close, as opposed to two or three months for conventional financing,” Harder said. “HUD takes a long time to move this process; they have outdated technology, and so one of the things we're working on is trying to fix the FHA process.” More housing construction ahead? Other proposals aim to mitigate the cost of construction, which “has just gone up and up and up,” according to Harder. “It's gotten more and more expensive to actually build a project, and so a lot of what we're trying to do is trying to make it cheaper to actually put a shovel in the dirt,” Harder said. One measure Harder thinks could be particularly impactful is “right to build zones” for multifamily housing. Jurisdictions that opt in will receive more federal support in exchange for changing their zoning to allow housing to be built by-right, so long as a project meets certain criteria. items.title: Upstate New York bucking national housing slowdown
items.description: The Northeast housing market is outperforming much of the rest of the country, and upstate New York is emerging as one of its hottest pockets, according to current HousingWire Data . Four upstate New York markets rank among HousingWire’s tightest in the Northeast — as Rochester stands out among metros with just 1.1 months of housing supply and a median 21 days to contract. The market has 1,024 active listings and a median list price of $289,000. Just 21% of listings have experienced price cuts, compared with 43% nationally. Syracuse, Buffalo-Niagara Falls and Binghamton also show tight inventory and relatively fast sales. For Eric O’Mara, broker-owner of Syracuse-based Integrated Real Estate , strength of the local and upstate New York market is evident in day-to-day transactions — even with activity evolving significantly since the pandemic-era boom. O’Mara said some homes still attract immediate attention, while others can languish when sellers push beyond what buyers consider reasonable. “The market here is elevated, and by elevated, what I mean is people are more knowledgeable about what they’re doing,” he told HousingWire. “You have some properties where they go on, and anyone and everyone can look at them and say, ‘Wow, that’s overpriced.’ Those are sitting. Then you still have some properties that go on — and they’re beautiful homes [priced right], and they’re selling in an hour.” Syracuse has 928 active listings , 1.6 months of supply and a $325,000 median list price, with homes moving in 42 days. Syracuse, Northeast market remain competitive HousingWire data shows 31.9% of Syracuse listings are experiencing price cuts — indicating that a significant share of sellers are adjusting their initial expectations. O’Mara said the overall market remains healthy, but both buyers and sellers have to account for conditions that are different from the pandemic years. “A lot of the time, they do still think it’s five years ago,” he said. “I talk to a lot of buyers, honestly, that are still holding off because they think the market’s going to cool down. “I don’t think it’s the market that is the problem. I think the market’s still very steady. “I think it’s going to consistently go up. I don’t think it’s going to spike like it did five years ago. It’s just going to be a steady rise, I would imagine for the next 20 years.” Across the broader Northeast, Hartford has 1.4 months of supply and a median 35 days to sale. Boston has 4,937 active listings, 1.8 months of supply and a median 35 days to sale despite an $895,000 median list price. Bridgeport-Stamford-Norwalk has a $989,000 median list price and 1.6 months of supply. Providence-New Bedford-Fall River has 2.1 months of supply, while Worcester has 1.8 months. The New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island metro has 20,191 active listings and 2.5 months of supply. Its $799,000 median list price and 56-day median time to sale still reflect tighter conditions than many Sun Belt markets. Regional strength is particularly notable with HousingWire Data showing national pending sales as down roughly 10% year-over-year. Expected population growth in Syracuse O’Mara pointed to both population growth and a lack of new housing construction as factors supporting local demand. “I don’t think there’s a lot of new builds here,” he said. “At least what I’m seeing is there’s only a handful of builders that are turning out a lot of houses every year, new builds in Syracuse. Rochester could be a little different. If you look out west — Salt Lake City and Scottsdale — and big cities out there, you’re looking at new neighborhoods every six months. items.title: Soaring Yields Strand REITs In M&A No-Man’s-Land
items.description: Soaring Yields Strand REITs In M A No-Man’s-Land October 6, 2026 | 7:52 pm ET Matt Wasielewski, National Treasury yields surging past 5% are shaping the REIT landscape, pulling dealmaking into a slowdown. With the 10‑year sitting at levels last seen in 2002 , REIT executives and analysts say the cost of capital has climbed so fast that buyers and sellers can’t agree on pricing, creating a gap wide enough to stall acquisitions across nearly every property type. REIT stocks are trading closer to their underlying asset values than they have in several years. The smaller discounts mean they aren’t cheap enough to become takeover targets, but they also aren’t valued richly enough to act as buyers, leaving the sector in a holding pattern until either rates stabilize or valuations diverge. “Any big deal in this environment has to maybe be reset, put on pause,” Haendel St. Juste , a REIT analyst at Mizuho Americas , said last week after Mizuho hosted its annual digital REIT conference. “I met some REIT management at our conference that said all of the acquisitions that they're doing are taking a pause.” Bisnow/created with Google Gemini The rising cost of debt is pushing buyers and sellers further apart, he said. “Buyers want higher cap rates because their cost of capital has gone up, and the sellers aren't really willing to sell at today's price — they want yesterday's price when debt costs were lower,” he said. REITs on average are trading at a roughly 10% discount to their net asset values, a narrower gap than the 15% to 30% that defined the sector in recent years, according to REIT-focused research and advisory firm Hoya Capital . That relatively modest gap between public and private market valuations is likely to put REIT M A activity into a holding pattern until REITs either gain enough value to become buyers or see their shares fall far enough that they become attractive buyout opportunities, Alex Pettee , director of research and ETFs at Hoya Capital, said in an email. “The question from here isn’t simply whether the 10-year goes higher. It’s whether public REITs hold their ground relative to private-market values,” he said. A handful of major deals have boosted M A totals even as total transaction counts remain relatively muted. AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed a blockbuster all-stock merger in August that created a multifamily REIT with 180,000 units and a $69B enterprise value. Smaller but still substantial deals this year include the $10.5B all-stock acquisition by Public Storage of National Storage Affiliates Trust and the plan to combine Independence Realty Trust with Centerspace into a 44,000-apartment REIT with an $8.1B valuation through another all-stock merger. That deal is facing opposition from a minority shareholder that wants IRT to instead consider selling itself. At least a dozen other REITs have either merged with competitors or been taken private in the last 12 months, according to an analysis by Bisnow . The pace of deals is being held back by the macroeconomic landscape, said Seth Laughlin, the head of real estate strategy and research at Cohen Steers. “Predicting M A is notoriously difficult — both from the macro and the micro — and I think there's periods of times when it just seems obvious," he said. “I wouldn't say we're in that time right now.” Interest rates need to find some semblance of stability before M A activity accelerates, especially buyouts that take REITs private, Laughlin said. Public markets have too much homogeneity in pricing inside asset classes, and public-to-public deals don’t look attractive without more price divergence. The takeouts happening in the public markets this year are focused on adding scale to unlock value as opposed to value-add acquisitions. items.title: Activist Investor Buys Stake In Empire State Building Owner
items.description: Activist Investor Buys Stake In Empire State Building Owner October 6, 2026 | 8:25 pm ET Ethan Rothstein, Deputy Managing Editor It's been a tough year for investors in Empire State Realty Trust , and a shake-up could be coming next. Activist investor Bruce Schanzer 's Erez Asset Management has acquired a 5.8% stake in ESRT, which owns the Empire State Building as well as a handful of office, retail and multifamily properties in Manhattan and Brooklyn, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Unsplash/Christian Ladewig The Empire State Building ESRT, whose shares are traded on the New York Stock Exchange, has lost roughly a third of its value this year. Its longtime cash cow, the Empire State Building 's observation deck, has struggled to retain visitors amid increasing competition. Two Erez entities disclosed that they paid $43M combined on Oct. 1 for a 5.8% stake in ESRT. Schanzer believes that ESRT's shares are “undervalued and represent an attractive investment opportunity,” according to the filing. ESRT's stock rose 4.7% in trading on Tuesday following the disclosure of Schanzer's stake. Schanzer was CEO of Long Island-based shopping center REIT Cedar Realty Trust for 11 years before founding Erez Asset Management in 2022. The company takes equity stakes in REITs and pushes their management to make changes to boost shareholder value. Erez has already reached out to ESRT's leadership “regarding capital allocation, business management and operations, and strategy and plans of [ESRT], including a potential strategic review of some or all of the Issuer's assets,” the filing states. Schanzer declined to comment beyond the filing and confirming that he acquired a 5.8% stake. An ESRT spokesperson didn't immediately respond to Bisnow 's request for comment. Empire State Realty Trust is led by chairman and CEO Anthony Malkin , the third generation of the Malkin family that has owned the Empire State Building since 1961. The REIT owns 7.5M SF of NYC office space, 800K SF of retail concentrated in Williamsburg and three apartment buildings totaling 743 units. But its performance is largely tied to its signature asset. ESRT wrote down the value of the Empire State Building observation deck by $166M in the second quarter amid a sluggish summer with dwindling profits. The net operating income of the asset fell from $24M to $12.4M year-over-year. The REIT's stock price fell 14% the day of the disclosure and had been steadily falling since before Erez's purchase. Its real estate portfolio, which had been struggling during the pandemic, has started to fill up again, with occupancy rising to 89.4% from 88.2% three months prior. It remains to be seen what changes Schanzer pushes for at ESRT amid a resurgent year for the city's real estate market. Retail occupancy in prime corridors is at a 10-year high, according to JLL , office rents are soaring, and vacancy in the city's rental market is below 2% . At another Erez target, manufactured home REIT UMH, Schanzer has been agitating for a board shake-up for months . A week ago, Erez launched a website called SaveUMH.com, with a presentation titled "Right Horse, Wrong Jockey.” “UMH owns a genuinely attractive portfolio in one of the most durable asset classes in real estate; those assets have grown dramatically in value over the last 20 years, none of which has been reflected in share price appreciation,” Schanzer wrote in a LinkedIn post . “The problem has never been the horse. It has been twenty years of mismanagement with a board that has provided insufficient oversight. Shareholders deserve better.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Contact Ethan Rothstein at ethan.rothstein@bisnow.com

items.title: How UK Investment Giant L&G Plans To Grow Its U.S. Multifamily Holdings
items.description: How UK Investment Giant L G Plans To Grow Its U.S. Multifamily Holdings October 6, 2026 | 7:06 pm ET Taylor Driscoll, Boston While the U.S. multifamily market has become less appealing to many investors, a London-based asset management giant is looking to capitalize on the lack of activity. L G Asset Management made its first investment in a new U.S. multifamily development in Concord, Massachusetts, in August, after investing in existing buildings in Denver and Chicago last year. The Concord project began construction last month, and the investor is now looking for more multifamily deals as the sector’s development has slowed due to elevated interest rates, rising construction costs and stagnant rents. Tim Watson, U.S. head of investment and portfolio management at L G, told Bisnow that the slowdown creates an opportunity for the firm to make long-term investments in supply-constrained markets. Courtesy of L G A September groundbreaking ceremony at 292-294 Baker Ave. in Concord "We expect to hold these assets for an incredibly long time," Watson said. “Where we're looking is where fundamentals and multifamily can remain strong for a long period of time, and where demand is going to essentially outweigh the amount of supply that can come on.” L G has $1.6T in assets under management globally, including $288B in the U.S. It manages pension plans for retirees, so holding assets for the long term can generate steady positive returns for those pension liabilities. Watson said the Concord project — a 201-unit building replacing part of an office park — was the perfect opportunity to fund a new development, as it's in a metropolitan area where housing construction has lagged while demand has remained steady. He said the lack of new construction in the market presents an opening to fund new development with less competition. "I certainly think it is absolutely an opportunity," he said. "We will deliver Concord into a market with not just no supply in Concord but very little supply, probably in the U.S. and certainly in the Boston area." Greater Boston has long been known as a high-barrier-to-entry market with strict municipal zoning and a lack of affordable developable land to make projects pencil. The firm’s partnership with Boston-based Taurus Investment Holdings and EcoSmart Solution helped it break into the market, as they had already gone through a lengthy entitlement and permitting process. "It just paints a broad picture of what we want to do in the U.S. and building partnerships and being in these communities," Watson said. It also helped that the project was proposed under the state's 40B affordable housing law, which allows a multifamily developer to circumvent some permitting restrictions as long as they set aside 25% of the units as income-restricted. Going forward, Watson said he expects L G will fund more acquisitions of existing multifamily assets than new developments, given the hurdles to starting construction. With the rising cost of debt , construction costs and regulatory burdens, Watson said his firm is being selective with new ground-up development projects. It is looking for "very unique submarkets, very unique builds, very unique partners that we can do this with." Landlords in many markets have been working through a glut of supply, especially in the Sun Belt region. And with higher-for-longer interest rates and construction costs that won't let up, multifamily development has been slowing across the country . "There's a reason there's things not getting built," Watson said. "There's all sorts of things that go in that make it relatively difficult to make these deals pencil, and so those are things that are relatively hard to overcome." items.title: Cambridge Residential Tower Secures $522M Loan: The Boston Deal Sheet
items.description: Cambridge Residential Tower Secures $522M Loan: The Boston Deal Sheet October 6, 2026 | 6:56 pm ET Taylor Driscoll, Boston A high-rise residential tower that opened four years ago in Kendall Square has landed a massive loan. Google Maps The 300-unit One65 Main in Kendall Square One65, a 25-story residential tower home to 300 apartments, locked down a $522M loan from BNP Paribas, according to an Oct. 2 mortgage record. The borrower was Willow Bridge Property Co., which manages the property and signed a ground lease for the site with Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Banker Tradesman first reported . MIT Investment Management Co. received approval for the project in 2019 and completed it in 2022 as part of the Kendall Square Initiative , which encompassed six buildings on Main Street and Broadway. The last site in the initiative, 200 Main Street, paused construction following the slowdown in the life sciences sector. The building was designed by Elkus Manfredi Architects and constructed by John Moriarty Associates. SALES Monarch Capital Partners acquired a 115K SF research and development and flex building at 115 and 117 Flanders Road in Westborough for almost $11M. The deal marks the first acquisition for the Boston-based firm. The deal was completed through a joint venture between Monarch and Lockspur Real Estate. The property is 52% leased, and the owners plan to complete a capital improvement program, including renovations to the lobbies, bathrooms and common areas, by the first quarter of 2027. CBRE served as the sales broker and arranged financing provided by TruNorth Bank. *** JLL Income Property Trust acquired the 396K SF Worcester Distribution Center in Boylston for $90M. The property was built in 2022 and is 100% leased to Cardinal Health. JLL IPT bought the warehouse at 80 Pine Hill Drive from NorthBridge Partners. LEASES Mass General Brigham signed a 105K SF lease at Greystar’s 74M lab building next to Assembly Row. MGB is the first tenant in the 469K SF lab building, which Greystar began developing in 2022. MGB plans to consolidate its pathology operations into the building and has the rights for future expansion. *** Walden Robotics signed a 50K SF lease at BioMed Realty’s 20 Sidney St. in University Park in Cambridge. The artificial intelligence robotics company is a spinout of Toyota Research Institute and in July announced a $300M funding round . FINANCING Google Earth IQHQ's Alewife Park District in 2024 IQHQ secured a $245M loan for its 27-acre Alewife Park campus in Cambridge. The loan was provided by Innovative Industrial Properties, a San Diego-based cannabis REIT. Part of the loan will help pay off the existing $85M bridge loan and will fund the completion of the rest of the project and its lease-up. The first phase of the project includes three buildings totaling 392K SF, with the second phase planned to include two other buildings up to 364K SF of development. Lila Therapeutics signed a 235K SF lease in the first phase of the project. *** Northwest Bank provided a $34M acquisition loan to Luzern Associates. The real estate firm acquired the Cherry Hill industrial portfolio in Danvers, consisting of three buildings across 200K SF. The property is fully occupied by medical device company Medtronic. CBRE and real estate law firm Bricker Graydon Wyatt advised on the deal. *** Berkeley Garbe secured a $35M financing package for 161 Concord Road in Billerica. The project is roughly 30% complete following the start of construction in June. Work on the 150K SF manufacturing building is expected to be completed in April 2027. MetLife Investment Management originated the loan. Hunneman’s Andrew Kaeyer led the team that arranged the transaction. Avison Young is the property’s exclusive leasing agent. *** WinnCos. scored $48M in financing for its 115-unit The Exchange multifamily development in Salem. The project is planned to be mixed-income, including 20 studios, 60 one-bedroom and 35 two-bedroom units.
